data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Photosynthesis supports most familiar food webs and replenishes atmospheric oxygen. Investigate how matter and energy contribute to plant growth.

1. Read **The Sugar Factory in Every Leaf**. Distinguish two material inputs from light energy, then identify the products.
2. Open the **Glossary** and win the **Word Scramble** — these words show up in everything else. Then win the **Memory** game.
3. Walk through **Follow One Carbon Atom** to see the order things happen.
4. Study the **Inputs and Outputs Map**, then try the sort: does each card go IN or OUT?
5. Take the quiz. Explain the evidence behind each answer.
6. Write your explanation with the **Sentence Frames**.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Sugar Factory** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Investigation: Which Light Grows a Plant?** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.
9. Read the **Four Things People Get Wrong** chart before the quiz — every one of those four is a common wrong answer.

Check the difference between matter and energy, and between observations and conclusions. 🌱☀️

Picture panels: Inputs and living leaves; Inside the leaf; Energy and respiration; Building living matter. Text-free illustrations use editable captions and image-specific descriptions. Diagrams simplify scale, anatomy and processes; colors and tokens are explained in captions. Follow the lesson text for scientific context. Educator review is pending.

history.title: The Sugar Factory in Every Leaf
history.data:
## The Sugar Factory in Every Leaf

A tree gains mass as it grows. Where does that new matter come from? Long ago, Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow and found that it gained much more mass than the soil lost. This was evidence against the idea that the tree simply ate the soil. It did not identify every source of its matter.

Carbon in plant sugars and wood comes from carbon dioxide in the air. Water supplies matter too. Fresh plants contain a great deal of water, and they need mineral nutrients. Sunlight supplies **energy**. It does not turn into the atoms in wood.

**Photosynthesis** uses light energy to build sugars. In plant cells, it takes place in **chloroplasts**. These structures contain **chlorophyll**, a green **pigment** that absorbs light. Leaves absorb red and blue light strongly. They absorb some green light too. Some green light bounces off or passes through, helping leaves look green. Green light is not useless.

A simple equation shows carbon dioxide and water going in. They are material **reactants**. Light supplies energy, not atoms. Sugars and oxygen are **products**. **Glucose** is the sugar used in our simple equation. The real process has many steps. The released oxygen comes from water. The carbon in sugar comes from carbon dioxide.

**Stomata** are tiny pores. Guard cells control their openings. Gases move through them, but water can leave too. The pattern of opening depends on the plant and its conditions. Some plants take in much of their carbon dioxide at night.

Plants use sugars to grow and store material. They also use them in cellular **respiration**, day and night. One form of respiration uses oxygen and transfers energy from sugar into forms cells can use. It releases carbon dioxide and water. It is not the same as breathing.

Photosynthesis needs suitable light. A lamp can provide it as well as the Sun. In darkness, stored material can support growth and respiration for a while. Light-driven sugar production cannot continue without light.

A plant releases oxygen overall when photosynthesis makes more than respiration uses. Bright light alone does not guarantee this. Water, temperature and carbon dioxide also matter.

Many algae and some bacteria use photosynthesis too. It supports most familiar food webs. Some other ecosystems use energy from chemical reactions instead. Compare a bean plant, an oak and algae: what do they share, and what differs?

data.progressionLabel: PROCESS: Carbon enters the leaf (Step 1) → Carbon becomes part of you (Step 7)

items.event: A carbon dioxide molecule drifts through the air and reaches a leaf surface.
The molecule passes through an open stoma into the inside of the leaf.
Chlorophyll and other pigments absorb light; leaves can use some green light as well as red and blue.
That captured energy powers a reaction between the carbon dioxide and water drawn up from the roots.
Water is split in light-driven reactions, releasing oxygen; linked reactions incorporate carbon dioxide into organic compounds used to make sugars.
Oxygen exits through the stomata into the air, and the glucose is stored or used to build plant tissue.
An animal eats the plant, and that same carbon atom becomes part of the animal's body.

questions.question: Where did the carbon atoms in an oak tree’s wood mainly come from?
options: Carbon dioxide from the air
Minerals and soil the roots ate
Water alone
Sunlight turning directly into wood

questions.question: Why do leaves look green?
options: Chlorophyll absorbs green light more strongly than all other colors
Some green light is reflected or transmitted; some is absorbed
Green is the color of the glucose stored inside the leaf cells
Minerals from the soil dye every part of the leaf bright green
questions.correctAnswer: Some green light is reflected or transmitted; some is absorbed

questions.question: Do plants perform cellular respiration?
options: No — respiration is only for animals
Only at night, when photosynthesis stops
Yes — day and night, using the sugar they made
Only when they are sick or dying
questions.correctAnswer: Yes — day and night, using the sugar they made

questions.question: Which list contains the two material inputs and the energy input for the simplified photosynthesis process?
options: Glucose, oxygen, water
Carbon dioxide, glucose, chlorophyll
Oxygen, light energy, soil minerals
Carbon dioxide, water, light energy

questions.question: A plant is kept in a dark closet with plenty of water. What happens to photosynthesis?
options: It continues at the same rate using stored sugar
It stops, because light energy is a required ingredient
It speeds up, because the plant is trying harder
It switches to using soil minerals instead of light
questions.correctAnswer: It stops, because light energy is a required ingredient

questions.question: What did van Helmont’s small soil-mass change suggest, and what could that experiment alone not establish?
questions.expectedAnswer: The small soil-mass loss did not account for the willow’s large gain, challenging the idea that the tree simply consumed soil. The experiment alone did not identify all matter sources or account fully for plant water content. Modern evidence shows carbon comes from carbon dioxide and water also contributes matter.

questions.question: Explain why photosynthesis matters to an animal that never eats plants — like a wolf.
questions.expectedAnswer: The wolf eats animals that ate plants, so the energy and carbon in its food originally came from photosynthesis. The wolf also breathes oxygen released by photosynthesis.

reflections.text: Which idea in this lesson was different from what you believed before? Describe what you used to think.

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 — Starting | 3 — Getting There | 5 — Scientist |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vocabulary | Everyday words only | 2-3 glossary terms used correctly | 4+ terms used correctly and precisely |
| Causal reasoning | States facts separately | Connects two ideas with because | Builds a full chain: ingredient to product to consequence |
| Accuracy | A major misconception remains | Mostly accurate, one slip | Every claim scientifically correct |

data.question: If plants make oxygen, do they suffocate at night? 🌙
data.answer: Plants keep respiring in darkness. They take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide. Photosynthesis needs suitable light, which may come from the Sun or a lamp.

data.question: Why are some leaves red or purple then? 🍁
data.answer: Other pigments can make leaves look red or purple. Chlorophyll is often still present and working too.

data.question: Could a plant live on a colored light — like only red?
data.answer: Yes, under suitable conditions. The amount of light reaching the leaves matters as well as its color. Equal lamp power or distance does not ensure equal useful light. Green light can help too.

data.question: Do plants in the ocean matter?
data.answer: Yes. Algae and some bacteria in the ocean use light to make organic matter and release oxygen. These tiny organisms help support ocean food webs. They are not all plants.

data.question: Is it true a plant is basically made of air? 💨
data.answer: The carbon in sugars and wood comes from the air. But plants also contain water and matter from water and minerals. “Made of air” leaves out those parts.

data.question: Why can't we just build machines that do photosynthesis?
data.answer: Researchers study ways to use light to make useful fuels. A leaf gives us ideas, but a machine need not copy every step. Making a useful system at large scale is a challenge.

history.title: Investigation: Which Light Grows a Plant?
history.meta: 7th Grade • Investigation brief • a colored-light experiment

data.title: Which Light Grows a Plant?
data.instructions: Compare plant growth under specified light treatments. Record potential confounding factors and distinguish growth observations from direct measurements of photosynthesis.
data.fitReason: Pigment absorption motivates predictions, but leaf and canopy behavior and photon delivery also affect growth. The investigation tests treatments under recorded conditions.

brief.context: A garden club wants to grow lettuce under indoor lamps. Someone suggests green light because plants look green. You have seeds, trays, red, blue, green and white LED strips, light boxes, a ruler and a scale. Compare the lamp setups for two weeks.
brief.audience: The gardening club deciding which LEDs to buy
brief.drivingQuestion: Under which lamp setup do the plants grow most in two weeks? What can this test tell us about light color?
brief.seedDirection: Predict what will happen. Leaves can use some green light. To test color alone, also match the amount of useful light reaching the leaves. Lamp power and distance are not enough to prove a match.
lockedLessonFacts: Photosynthesis needs carbon dioxide, water, and light energy; it produces glucose and oxygen.
Leaves absorb strongly in red and blue regions and also absorb some green light; some green is reflected or transmitted.
A plant kept in the dark cannot photosynthesize and grows pale and weak even with water.
Plants also respire day and night, releasing energy from the sugar they made.
Carbon in sugars comes from carbon dioxide; water also contributes matter and fresh mass includes water.
openQuestions: How will we keep water, temperature, starting plants and hours of light the same?
Will we measure height, leaf count or mass? What does each measure leave out?
Can we borrow a sensor to match the useful light at leaf level? If not, how will we explain that limit?
How will we use several seedlings so one unusual plant does not decide the result?
stakeholders: The gardening club paying for LEDs
The custodian who controls room temperature
Anyone who will eat the lettuce
criteria: Use the same water, temperature, starting plants and hours of light.
Use at least four seedlings for each setup.
Measure in the same way on the same days.
If useful light is not measured and matched, compare lamp setups, not color alone.
Compare results with your prediction and use four glossary words correctly.
constraints: Use the listed tools; ask the teacher about a suitable light sensor.
Check and water trays every school day.
Height may show stretching, and fresh mass includes water. Neither directly measures how fast photosynthesis occurs.
brief.deliverable: Share a test plan, a prediction, a two-week data table and a recommendation. Explain the results and name what the test cannot show.

parallelExample.context: A greenhouse wondered whether extra CO2 in the air made tomatoes grow faster.
parallelExample.move: Growers split identical plants into two rooms that differed only in CO2 level, kept light and water the same, weighed the harvest, and found the higher-CO2 room grew more. Because one thing changed, the result meant something.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: Same discipline: change exactly one input to photosynthesis and measure the output. Your input is light color instead of CO2.

supports.frameStarter: We predict ____ light will grow the most because chlorophyll ____. We will keep ____, ____, and ____ the same.
frameChoices: Compare red, blue, green, and white light
Compare white light to a red-plus-blue mix
Compare green light to darkness to see whether green does anything at all
Compare two brightness levels of the same color
coachPrompts: If the green tray grows a little, what does that tell you about 'reflects green'?
Which observations show growth or stretching, and why do they not directly measure photosynthetic rate?
What would make the club's decision wrong even if your data is right?

data.coachHint: Equal distance and electrical power do not ensure equal photon delivery. Without that control, compare the tested lamps and disclose the limitation.
data.sourceExcerpt: Leaves absorb some green light as well as red and blue. To test spectrum, account for photon delivery, duration, plant conditions and the difference between growth and photosynthetic rate.
